summary: Mounir Mouawad presents his transition from product management at Amazon (UK deals program for Black Friday and Prime Day), Google (Google Pay in 30 AMIA markets), and Stripe (Bank as a Service for AMIA) to co-founding Porsche AI with Emma, whom he met at Stripe. Porsche AI is an open-source SDK for building production agents targeting regulated industries. The talk focuses on four key differences between Big Tech product work and AI startup building. First, user discovery in AI feels fundamentally different. Unlike Big Tech, where user problems have shape and adjacency to known problems, AI user problems are emergent—users know they want AI but cannot yet define their problems. He compares this to configuring a character in a Soulslike game (Neo): directionally you know stats need to go up but cannot figure out how. The anchor becomes hypothesis-driven deliberate iteration rather than conventional three-to-six-month roadmaps. Second, traditional user storyboards and critical user journeys largely disappear. He likens this to No Man's Sky, where you start with no story arc and must create your own narrative. Founders must help users overcome initial inertia around AI adoption, co-creating use-case narratives before gradually reaching more familiar territory where problems become scoped and tangible. Third, product development is deeply gratifying. Instead of coordinating across dozens of departments for sign-offs (the 'hurting lemmings' sensation of Big Tech), a founder can go from idea to spec to release in hours or days. However, in AI, velocity is table stakes—not a luxury. Technological breakthroughs like MCP, agent-to-agent protocols, and diffusion models create fleeting windows demanding rapid reaction. Fourth, the hardest challenge is the lack of scaffolding for outreach, awareness, traffic, and adoption. Without a major brand, it feels like playing Crash Bandicoot without boosters or Mario Kart without weapons. Key lessons include recognizing that people follow people (unlike Stripe where a Collison tweet suffices), finding credible industry advocates as force multipliers, and partnering with peer or slightly-ahead startups for cross-marketing, cross-selling, and integration doc placements (e.g., Browserbase).

takeaways: AI user problems are emergent and undefined; users know they want AI but cannot articulate specific problems, requiring hypothesis-driven iteration instead of conventional roadmaps.
Traditional user storyboards and critical user journeys largely disappear; founders must co-create narratives with users to overcome initial AI adoption inertia.
Product development velocity in AI startups is table stakes, not a nice-to-have; missing rapid-release capability means losing fleeting technological windows.
Technological breakthroughs like MCP, agent-to-agent protocols, and diffusion models create short-lived opportunities that demand immediate product responses to cement developer community standing.
Building awareness without Big Tech brand scaffolding is the steepest learning curve; people follow people, so finding credible advocates is essential.
Strategic partnerships with peer startups—including cross-marketing, cross-selling, and integration doc placements—are critical channels for a new startup's discovery.
Going from idea to released product in hours or days is exhilarating but requires disciplined speed, unlike Big Tech's multi-department sign-off process.

sections.title: Introduction and Big Tech Background
sections.summary: Mounir introduces himself as CEO and co-founder of Porsche AI, an open-source SDK for production agents in regulated industries, co-founded with Emma from Stripe. He reviews his Big Tech career: launching Amazon UK deals (Black Friday, Prime Day), Google Pay across 30 AMIA markets, and Bank as a Service at Stripe for AMIA. He always wanted to start his own company and felt it was a copout not to.

sections.title: User Problems and Discovery in AI
sections.summary: Explains how AI user discovery differs from Big Tech. In Big Tech, user problems have shape and adjacency to known problems. In AI, users know they want AI but cannot define their problems—they are emergent properties of the space. Compares this to a Soulslike game (Neo) where you cannot figure out how to configure your character. The anchor becomes hypothesis-driven deliberate iteration rather than conventional roadmaps.

sections.title: Co-Creating User Narratives Without Storyboards
sections.summary: Traditional user storyboards and critical user journeys largely go out the window. Compares this to No Man's Sky where there is no story arc at the start. Founders must help users overcome initial inertia, co-create narratives, and anchor on use cases before gradually reaching familiar territory with scoped, tangible problems.

sections.title: Product Development Velocity as Table Stakes
sections.summary: Product development in a startup is deeply gratifying compared to Big Tech's multi-department sign-off process (the 'hurting lemmings' sensation). You can go from idea to release in hours or days. However, in AI, velocity is table stakes—not a nice-to-have. Breakthroughs like MCP, agent-to-agent protocols, and diffusion models create fleeting windows requiring rapid reaction to cement your standing in the developer community.

sections.title: Building Awareness Without Brand Scaffolding
sections.summary: The hardest challenge: lack of scaffolding for outreach, awareness, traffic, and adoption. Compares to playing Crash Bandicoot without boosters or Mario Kart without weapons. Key lessons: people follow people (unlike Stripe where a Collison tweet suffices), find credible industry advocates as force multipliers, and partner with peer or slightly-ahead startups for cross-marketing, cross-selling, and integration doc placements (e.g., Browserbase). Closes by inviting LinkedIn conversations and GitHub stars.
